newsitem.title: USA: MORTGAGE MARKET LOSE MOST GAINS AS TREASURIES SINK.
newsitem.headline: MORTGAGE MARKET LOSE MOST GAINS AS TREASURIES SINK.

text.p: Mortgage-backed securities (MBS) gave up nearly all of the morning's steep gains by midday Wednesday, reflecting a soured Treasury market rally.

The market, seen as highly vulnerable as analysts try to discern near-term Federal Reserve interest rate policy, failed to sustain the upward momentum generated by moderate July economic and inflation reports.
MBS that had been up as much as 5/8 point early Wednesday were 1/8 to 1/4 point firmer at midday. Ten-year Treasury notes were up 1/4 at 98-07/32.

The 6.37 percent yield on 10-year notes was still much higher than the 6.00 percent low reached about two weeks ago, several traders noted. They said they doubted rates would soon fall back to the 6.00 percent level and reignite waves of home refinancing and premature MBS repayments.

July Producer Price Index data quelled some inflation fears. A record seventh straight decline was reported in overall PPI. Both the overall and the core reading, which excludes food and energey prices, fell 0.1 percent in July compared with 0.1 percent gains predicted by a Reuters poll of economists.
Retail sales rose 0.6 percent overall and 0.5 percent when auto sales were factored out. A Reuters poll found average estimated gains of 0.7 percent overall and 0.5 percent excluding autos.

Among 30-year 7 1/2-percent MBS, Government National Mortgage Association bonds were up 7/32 at 100-26/32, Freddie Mac bonds were also 7/32 higher at 101-02/32 and Fannie Maes were up 9/32 at 100-30/32.

Market participants were turning their attention to Thursay's reports of July consumer prices, industrial production and the latest Mortgage Bankers Association weekly refinancing and home purchase data.

Analysts at PaineWebber Inc, in a new research report, advised that "it's a good time to be buying seasoned CMOs (collateralized mortgage obligations); they look cheap to both new WAM (weighted average maturity) product and the new and seasoned collateral."
They added that it was "particularly tempting for index players to substitute seasoned CMOs for seasoned collateral; neither rolls, and the former represents better value."
